We've introduced the general idea of null hypothesis significance testing in the past few chapters, and we used the $z$ statistic to complete some hypothesis tests. Here we'll introduce a new test statistic, the $t$ test. We'll see how it differs from a $z$ statistic--which is not very much at all, thankfully. It's just used in slightly different circumstances. We'll reintroduce the ideas of sample variance and degrees of freedom because they will be newly relevant thanks to this $t$ statistic. And we'll practice hypothesis testing with the $t$ test.

## What if we don't know the population variability?

We started the previous chapter by taking some samples from a full deck of cards. Since we knew the composition of the deck, we could figure out the population standard deviation, $\sigma$. With that in hand we could compute the standard error of the mean, $\sigma_M$, which contributed to both the confidence interval and the $z$-test statistic.

Let's take some samples from a new deck. But this isn't a regular, complete deck. I took some cards out. Which ones? I didn't even look! So the characteristics of the population are now a mystery: we don't know $\mu$, or the true standard deviation, $\sigma$. What are we to do? Let's compare two potential samples. As before, we put each card back and shuffle before drawing the next one.

::: {#quiz-t-sample-variability}
{{< include quizzes/11-t-test-card-samples.qmd >}}
:::

We find ourselves now in a more typical situation now. It's rare that we know the population standard deviation; the procedures from the past few chapters which rely on knowing $\sigma$ provide the foundations of what is to come, but we can't actually use them very often in practice. Thankfully, we don't have to throw out everything we've learned and start from scratch. Rather, we just let our sample do a little more work. We can use our sample's variability to estimate the population variability. And that means we have to account for the fact that our estimate of uncertainty is itself uncertain.

The question of uncertainty matters for both confidence intervals and hypothesis tests. To put an interval around a sample mean, or to judge how far it is from a hypothesized mean, we need a standard error. But what if we don't know the population standard deviation?

## From $z$ to $t$

Here's the inferential process diagram I showed for the $z$-test a few chapters ago. In that example, we treated the original population's mean and standard deviation as known.

::: {#fig-t-known-population}
{{< interactive-figure tKnownPopulationDiagram makeInferentialDiagram options='{"preset":"z-test","maxWidth":"42rem","ariaLabel":"The treatment-study design used for the z test: the original population mean and standard deviation are known. We observe the treated sample mean and sample size, and infer the treated population mean."}' fallback="Known original population μ and σ; treated sample M and n; inference from the treated sample to its population." >}}

The original population's mean and variability are known. The treated sample is our clue to the unknown treated population.
:::

We use a single-sample $t$ test to compare a population mean with a specified reference value when we don't know the population standard deviation. The reference value is our null hypothesis, not necessarily a population fact we already know.

::: {#fig-t-estimated-population}
{{< interactive-figure singleTInferentialDiagram makeInferentialDiagram options='{"preset":"single-t","maxWidth":"42rem","labels":{"original-population":["Reference","population","Specified μ₀","Unknown σ"],"treated-sample":["Treated sample","M, n, and s"]},"ariaLabel":"The same treatment-study layout with population standard deviation unknown. The null specifies a reference mean μ₀; the treated sample now supplies s as well as M and n. We estimate standard error from s and n."}' fallback="Specified reference mean μ₀ and unknown σ; treated sample M, n, and s; the sample now supplies an estimate of variability too." >}}

The inferential logic is the same. We still have a reference mean, but population variability is now unknown. The sample supplies $s$ as well as its mean and size.
:::

These diagrams show a treatment study. The statistical comparison doesn't by itself establish that a treatment caused a difference, and a single-sample $t$ test doesn't require a treatment at all, as we'll see with the class reaction times.

As an example, we might want to test whether the average sleep duration of a population differs from eight hours. Eight hours is a stipulated reference value, not necessarily a fact about the population mean. In Chapter 10 we did this with the $z$-test; we were able to use the $z$-statistic because we assumed that the population standard deviation was known---I just made up a standard deviation of 1.5 hours. Best not to just make things up, though. At least not when we don't have to. And we had something all along that we could use instead: the *sample's* standard deviation. We can use that to estimate the population standard deviation. We can use basically the same logic as the $z$-test to perform a hypothesis test without ever knowing for sure the population standard deviation. The resulting test statistic is no longer a $z$ statistic. The value gets a new name: a $t$-statistic. And the reference distribution is no longer the standard normal distribution, but a $t$ distribution.

{{< include quizzes/10-confidence-intervals-design.qmd >}}

### The $t$ statistic

Remember that the $z$ test compares our sample mean with the mean specified by the null hypothesis, $\mu_0$, in units of standard error:

$$ z = \frac{M - \mu_0}{\sigma_M}, \qquad \sigma_M = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} $$

It's the denominator here, the standard error of the mean, that describes the variability of the sampling distribution. So to use this $z$ test, we have to know the population standard deviation, $\sigma$. Most often in real research we don't know it, and so our $z$ test statistic is missing its denominator.

Thankfully, this isn't just a dead end. There is a very simple solution.

### Estimated standard error

The solution to not knowing the population standard deviation is simply to use our sample's standard deviation to estimate it. Instead of our denominator being the known standard error of the mean, $\sigma_M$, we call it the estimated standard error of the mean, $s_M$. You'll remember that Greek symbols are usually used to refer to population parameters and letters for sample statistics.

<!-- DRAFT: Return briefly to the two hands: same n, so the more variable hand supplies the larger estimated SE. Using s solves the missing-denominator problem, but s itself changes from sample to sample. Establish that extra uncertainty before naming the new reference distribution. -->

### Formulas for standard error and estimated standard error

| | Population variability known | Population variability estimated |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Standard error | $\sigma_M = \dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$ | $s_M = \dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}}$ |
| Test statistic | $z = \dfrac{M - \mu_0}{\sigma_M}$ | $t = \dfrac{M - \mu_0}{s_M}$ |

So this is the fundamental difference between the $z$ statistic and the $t$ statistic. The numerator is the same. The denominator still describes uncertainty in the mean, but now we have to estimate it.

You might say the $t$ test is just the $z$ test in a different pair of pants. But the change has a consequence: the denominator now varies from sample to sample too. We need to account for that when deciding how unusual a test statistic is.

### Degrees of freedom revisited

Remember that to calculate sample variance, we first calculate the sample mean. The deviations from that mean sum to zero, so only $n - 1$ of them are free to vary.

$$ s^2 = \frac{\sum(X-M)^2}{n-1}, \qquad s_M = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}, \qquad df = n-1 $$

Dividing by $n-1$ corrects the downward bias in the sample variance. But it doesn't make any particular sample's estimate exact. That remaining uncertainty is what the $t$ distribution accounts for.

For this single-sample $t$ test, $df = n - 1$. Other kinds of $t$ tests can have different degrees of freedom, as we'll see in the next chapters.

<!-- DRAFT: Add a short historical paragraph here, now that the small-sample problem is clear: William Sealy Gosset's work at Guinness, his 1908 publication under the name Student, and the origin of "Student's t." Keep the practical small-sample motivation central. Sources and attribution notes are in the private structural-pass record. -->

## The $t$ distribution

With the $z$ test, we used the standard normal distribution to judge the standardized test statistic. That reference curve stays the same as sample size changes, even though the standard error of the mean changes.

The $t$ distribution is a family of distributions. There's a slightly different $t$ curve for each value of degrees of freedom. With low degrees of freedom, the curve has heavier tails than the standard normal curve: extreme standardized statistics are more common because we are dividing by an uncertain estimate of standard error. As degrees of freedom increase, the curve approaches the standard normal curve.

These curves describe the test statistic under the null hypothesis, assuming independent observations from a normal population. They aren't distributions of individual reaction times, or of sample means in milliseconds.

### How the $t$ distribution changes with degrees of freedom

The graph below shows how the $t$ distribution changes along with degrees of freedom, with the standard normal distribution shown for reference. The shape changes quickly at very low degrees of freedom, but the change slows down as degrees of freedom increase.

::::: {.callout-tip .interactive}

In other words, there is a big difference between the distributions for degrees of freedom of one and two, or four and five, but a comparatively small difference between the distributions for twenty-eight and twenty-nine or twenty-nine and thirty degrees of freedom.

## The $t$ Table

So now that we know about the properties of the distribution, particularly how it depends on degrees of freedom, we're ready to start thinking about probabilities. With the normal distribution and the $z$ test, we could determine the area under the curve for, say, the most extreme five percent of the distribution. And we want to do exactly the same thing for the $t$ distribution. The only difference is that, again, there is more than one $t$ distribution. And so the specific probabilities depend on the degrees of freedom.

So instead of referring to the unit normal table like we've done in the past, we refer to a $t$ table. Like the unit normal table, this will give us the $t$ values associated with different regions of the distribution. But unlike the unit normal table, the $t$ table must include values for different degrees of freedom.

{{< interactive-figure staticTTable makeTTable options='{"title":"t critical values","df":{"from":1,"to":30},"alphas":[0.1,0.05,0.025,0.01,0.005],"confidence":false,"interactive":false}' fallback="Static table of t critical values." >}}

So typically the table looks something like this. There's a column for degrees of freedom, followed by columns for different alpha values of .1, .05, and so on. And often it'll give these values for both one-tailed and two-tailed hypotheses. Use the heading for your chosen tail and alpha: one-tailed .05 or two-tailed .05, for example. Then you find the right row based on your degrees of freedom, which for a single-sample $t$ test is one less than your sample size.

::::: {.callout-tip .interactive}
## Connect the table to the critical regions

{{< interactive-figure tCriticalValueTable makeTTable options='{"title":"t critical values","df":{"from":1,"to":30},"alphas":[0.1,0.05,0.025,0.01,0.005],"confidence":true,"selectedTail":"two","selected":{"df":22,"tail":"two","alpha":0.05},"tableMaxHeight":"18rem"}' fallback="Interactive t critical-value table." >}}

{{< interactive-figure tCriticalCurve makeDistributionGraph options='{"color":"var(--sfs-null-color, currentColor)","distribution":"t","df":{"$value":"tCriticalValueTable.df"},"title":{"$template":"df = ${tCriticalValueTable.df}"},"style":"minimal","height":160,"xDomain":[-4,4],"yDomain":[0,0.45],"xTicks":5,"shade":{"$value":"tCriticalValueTable.shade"},"maxWidth":"24rem"}' fallback="t distribution curve with the selected critical region shaded." >}}

:::: {.callout-footer}
::: {.tutorial-step data-title="Two-tailed" data-action='{"df":22,"tail":"two","alpha":0.05,"animate":false}'}
For a sample of 23 observations, $n = 23$, so $df = 22$. With a two-tailed $\alpha = .05$, the critical values are about $\pm 2.07$.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="Smaller df" data-action='{"df":10,"tail":"two","alpha":0.05,"animate":true}'}
With fewer degrees of freedom, the same two-tailed alpha level needs a larger critical value because the $t$ distribution has heavier tails.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="One-tailed" data-action='{"df":22,"tail":"right","alpha":0.05,"animate":true}'}
For a one-tailed $\alpha = .05$ test with the same degrees of freedom, all of the critical area is on one side.
:::
::::
:::::

## Assumptions of the single-sample $t$ test

The exact $t$ reference distribution assumes independent observations from a normal population. With larger samples, the procedure can tolerate some departures from normality, but there is no automatic cutoff at $n=30$. Strong skew and extreme observations deserve attention, especially in small samples.

Independence means that observations do not supply overlapping information. Random sampling helps support inference to a population; representativeness concerns which population the sample can reasonably tell us about. A larger sample doesn't automatically repair dependence or selection bias.

<!-- DRAFT: Keep this short and connect it to the coming data inspection. No equal-variance assumption is needed between a reference population and a treated population for this one-sample test; introduce equality of two variances only with the pooled test in Chapter 12. -->

## Hypothesis tests, step by step: class reaction times

So now we'll work through an example hypothesis test using our new tool, the $t$ test. For the purposes of the example, we'll use data collected by a statistics class using the reaction time test from our Spider-People example.

In Chapter 8, I supplied a population standard deviation of 50 milliseconds. But now let's not pretend to know that population standard deviation. We'll estimate the standard error using the class's variability, and compare the mean with the same website reference of 284 milliseconds.

This is a worked analysis of existing data. In a planned test, we'd specify the hypotheses and decision criteria before looking at the results, as in Chapter 8.

### Step 1: State the hypotheses

We'll use a nondirectional hypothesis: the population mean differs from the reference in either direction.

$$ H_0: \mu = 284\text{ ms} \qquad H_1: \mu \ne 284\text{ ms} $$

Here 284 is the stipulated benchmark. Whether this class represents a broader population of students is a separate question from the calculation.

### Step 2: Set the decision criteria

We'll use $\alpha = .05$ for a two-tailed test. With 65 scores, $df = 64$, so the critical values are approximately $\pm 1.998$. We reject the null if $t < -1.998$ or $t > 1.998$.

::: {#tbl-t-class-critical}
{{< interactive-figure classRtCriticalTable makeTTable options='{"title":"Critical values for the class test","df":{"from":62,"to":66},"alphas":[0.1,0.05,0.025,0.01,0.005],"tableMinWidth":"0","maxWidth":"32rem","confidence":false,"interactive":false,"selected":{"df":64,"tail":"two","alpha":0.05}}' fallback="t table excerpt for 62 through 66 degrees of freedom, highlighting the two-tailed .05 critical value of 1.998 at df = 64." >}}

An excerpt of the $t$ table, with the $df = 64$ row highlighted. The two-tailed $.05$ heading puts $.025$ in each tail.
:::

Here are the scores, in milliseconds:

The histogram is somewhat uneven. A small sample's histogram doesn't establish the shape of its population. We'll use the $t$ model for this practice analysis, keeping the small sample and the sampling method in mind when interpreting it.

| Quantity | Symbol | Class data |
|:--|:--|--:|
| Sample size | $n$ | 65 |
| Sample mean | $M$ | 298.18 ms |
| Sample standard deviation | $s$ | 47.76 ms |
| Null reference mean | $\mu_0$ | 284 ms |
| Degrees of freedom | $df = n-1$ | 64 |

$$ s_M = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}} = \frac{47.76}{\sqrt{65}} \approx 5.923\text{ ms} $$

<!-- DRAFT: Brief reminder that s comes from the raw scores using n-1. Consider an optional calculation check for s or SE here; keep the existing t-statistic quiz as the next step, rather than giving its answer first. -->

$$ t = \frac{M-\mu_0}{s_M} = \frac{298.18-284}{5.923} $$

{{< include quizzes/11-t-test-t-statistic.qmd >}}

### Step 4: Make a decision

You should have calculated $t \approx 2.39$. Our sample mean is about 2.39 estimated standard errors above the null reference. This exceeds the upper critical value of 1.998, so we reject the null hypothesis.

{{< interactive-figure classRtTestDecision makeDistributionGraph options='{"color":"var(--sfs-null-color, currentColor)","distribution":"t","df":64,"title":"Null distribution: df = 64","style":"minimal","xAxis":true,"yLabel":false,"xDomain":[-4,4],"xTicks":5,"labels":{"x":"t statistic"},"shade":{"tail":"two","alpha":0.05},"markers":[{"at":-1.99773,"label":"−1.998","height":0.6,"color":"var(--sfs-critical-color, #c63f3f)"},{"at":1.99773,"label":"+1.998","height":0.6,"color":"var(--sfs-critical-color, #c63f3f)"},{"at":2.394714,"label":"t = 2.39","height":0.6,"color":"var(--sfs-accent, #2c7fb8)"}],"maxWidth":"42rem"}' fallback="Null t distribution with 64 degrees of freedom. The two rejection regions lie beyond ±1.998; the observed t of 2.39 is in the right rejection region." >}}

The equivalent two-tailed $p$-value, calculated with software using the unrounded statistic, is approximately $.020$. As in Chapter 8, this includes outcomes at least as extreme in either direction. Our critical-value table locates the rejection boundary; it doesn't give this exact $p$-value.

## Effect size and confidence interval

### How big is the difference?

We can use a version of Cohen's $d$ for the single-sample $t$ test, just as we did with the $z$ test. The difference here is that we use sample standard deviation ($s$) in place of the unknown population standard deviation ($\sigma$).

$$ M-\mu_0 = 14.18\text{ ms}, \qquad d = \frac{M-\mu_0}{s} = \frac{298.18-284}{47.76} \approx 0.30 $$

<!-- DRAFT: One brief interpretation: the sample mean is 14.18 ms slower than the reference, about .30 sample SDs above it. Recall Chapter 9: magnitude and practical importance are separate from significance; report magnitude and uncertainty regardless of the test decision. -->

### A confidence interval for the mean

<!-- DRAFT: Short application of Chapter 10's construction. Same estimate ± margin of error, now using estimated SE and a t critical value with n-1 df. No new derivation of confidence intervals needed. -->

$$ M \pm t^*s_M = 298.18 \pm 1.998(5.923) \approx [286.35,\ 310.02]\text{ ms} $$

| Estimate | 95% confidence interval |
|:--|:--|
| Population mean reaction time | $[286.35,\ 310.02]$ ms |
| Difference from the 284 ms reference | $[2.35,\ 26.02]$ ms |

::: {#fig-t-class-ci}
{{< interactive-figure classRtConfidenceInterval makeIntervalDiagram options='{"distribution":"t","m":298.1846153846154,"s":47.7552000793148,"n":65,"confidence":95,"reference":284,"xDomain":[275,320],"units":"Mean reaction time (ms)"}' fallback="95% t confidence interval for the mean: 286.35 to 310.02 ms, with point estimate 298.18 ms. The reference mean of 284 ms lies below the entire interval." >}}

The 95% $t$ interval excludes the reference mean of 284 ms, agreeing with the two-tailed test at $\alpha = .05$.
:::

<!-- DRAFT: Recall coverage and sampling/measurement limitations. At the same numerical SE, t* gives a wider interval than z*; a t interval need not be wider if the SE also changes. -->

## Reporting and interpreting the results

### Reporting results

There's a fairly standard way of reporting a hypothesis test. Here's an example based on our class reaction time data:

> A two-tailed single-sample $t$ test comparing the class reaction times ($M = 298.18$ ms, $SD = 47.76$ ms) with a reference of 284 ms was statistically significant, $t(64) = 2.39$, $p = .020$, $d = 0.30$. The estimated mean difference was 14.18 ms, with a 95% confidence interval of [2.35, 26.02] ms.

There's a lot of information packed into this fairly short, dry, technical statement. You should report the kind of hypothesis test, the null reference, the descriptive statistics, the test statistic and its degrees of freedom in parentheses, the $p$ value, and the estimated magnitude and uncertainty.

### Interpreting the results

If we wanted to get headlines, maybe we could say something like "statistics makes your brain work slower." But this class wasn't randomly assigned to study statistics, and the reference value isn't a randomized comparison group.

Or maybe a lot of people on that website take the test a bunch of times, and maybe their reaction times got a little faster with practice, so maybe our class was just unpracticed at this task rather than slower in general. Or maybe we're making a Type I error. This is a good lesson on why a "statistically significant" result doesn't by itself explain the difference or establish how widely it generalizes.

## Statistical power with a $t$ test

Remember the two sampling distributions from Chapter 9. The null curve is centered on 284 ms. For the alternative, suppose the true population mean were 298.18 ms—the mean we observed in our class. The purple area shows the chance of rejecting the null if that hypothetical alternative were true.

::: {#fig-t-power}
{{< interactive-figure tPowerIllustration makeStatisticalPowerDiagram options='{"schematic":true,"mu":284,"sigma":47.7552000793148,"n":65,"diff":14.1846153846154,"alpha":0.05,"showControls":[],"distribution":"t","key":false,"axisRaw":true,"axisLabel":"Mean reaction time (ms)","regionValues":true}' fallback="Schematic null and alternative t curves (df = 64) centered on 284 and 298.18 ms. Power is the shaded area under the alternative beyond the null rejection boundaries, about .654; beta is the area between them, about .346." >}}

A reminder of the logic of power: the rejection regions come from the null model, but power is an area under the alternative. These schematic $t$ curves illustrate that logic; they aren't an exact $t$-power calculation.[^t-power-approximation]
:::

[^t-power-approximation]: <!-- DRAFT: Footnote on the approximation. Facts: the figure slides a copy of the null t curve (df = 64) over to the alternative and gives power = .654 (beta = .346). That is the usual "swap in the critical t" approximation. Exact t-test power uses the noncentral t distribution, which software (R's power.t.test, G*Power) reports as .655 here, so a reader's software may differ in the third decimal. The gap grows with smaller samples (e.g., n = 15, d = 0.5: .420 approximate vs .438 exact). -->

Using the observed mean to position this hypothetical alternative doesn't tell us the true population mean, or how convincing this completed study was. For planning a future study, we'd specify a plausible effect to detect.
